source.title: Who Pays and How Much
source.summary: Tax incidence, deadweight loss, and how Islamic tax instruments compare to modern systems.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Taxes change behavior. Income taxes discourage earning; sales taxes discourage spending; property taxes discourage holding. The economics of tax design is about minimizing these distortions while raising enough revenue. This episode covers tax incidence (who really bears the burden), deadweight loss, and the efficiency-equity tradeoff. Then it examines Islamic tax instruments: zakat as a wealth tax with a 2.5% rate and nisab threshold, kharaj as a land/output tax, ushur as a trade levy. Each has specific economic properties. Zakat's flat rate is simple but possibly insufficient for a modern state. The jizya receives an honest treatment: discriminatory by modern standards, though it had a specific fiscal logic in its historical context.

x.single_post: Medieval sultans charged merchants 5% to cross their lands. Medieval caliphs charged farmers based on their harvest. Both understood what modern tax theory calls deadweight loss. Zakat remains a 2.5% wealth tax.

linkedin.post: Tax design has always been about balancing efficiency with revenue needs. Medieval Islamic rulers understood this intuitively. Zakat functions as a wealth tax at 2.5% with a nisab threshold. Kharaj targets agricultural output and land productivity. Ushur applies to trade flows at borders. Each instrument addresses what economists now call tax incidence and deadweight loss—concepts that were embedded in fiscal policy 1,300 years ago. The efficiency-equity tradeoff that dominates modern tax debates was already being navigated in 7th-century economic policy. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-2
